records.title: Erika Armstrong • 3-й+
records.text: I'm so thankful I caught the tail end of the glory days of aviation. There was a time when stepping onto a plane meant something, when the flight deck held a full crew and flying still carried a sense of adventure, romance, and ceremony. My generation wants to believe pilotless cockpits will never happen, but I think that's just our Gen X mindset talking. We came of age when the three-person flight deck was still a thing (captain, first officer, flight engineer) and watched, in real time, as that number got whittled down to two. We know firsthand how essential that third set of eyes and hands was, right up until the airlines decided it wasn't. And here's the uncomfortable part: within a generation, it felt normal that two pilots were enough. So when I insist "they'll never get rid of the second pilot," I have to ask: isn't that exactly what someone in the three-pilot era would have said about the flight engineer? Am I still a realist by treating the two-pilot cockpit as sacred, or am I being nostalgic, mistaking the last configuration I personally lived through for a natural limit rather than just another checkpoint on a long trend line toward fewer pilots, and eventually, however uncomfortable it is to say, none at all... https://lnkd.in/gQQM9D68 Joby Aviation #aviation #history #aviationhistory #pilot #pilottraining #fly #flight #information #conversation #discussion #achickinthecockpit #pilotlife #airlines #airplane #aircraft #autonomous #engineering #innovation #learn #

records.title: Erika Armstrong • 3-й+
records.text: There are words and expressions that are bandied about - “safe” and “fully-qualified” come to mind - that are poorly understood, IMHO. In re the first word - “safe” - I believe that there are such things as more-safe and less-safe; I don’t believe there exists anything that is completely-safe. And people make decisions about activities using an internal judgment of “safe enough.” We drive cars toward other cars with a combined velocity of over 100 mph, divided by a yellow stripe or a dashed white line painted on the highway surface. We have very little idea what is happening in the other vehicle - screaming kids, teenagers texting, and worse…and yet we consider it safe enough. “Fully-qualified” is another expression used to describe, in this context, the two current occupants of an airline cockpit. People, understandably, assume that the FAA is making sure that the airline is making sure that the simulator instructors are making sure that the new pilot - captain or first officer - is “fully-qualified.” How would we describe these pilots after years in real world airline operations - “Way-qualified?” “Outrageously-qualified?” (There's more, which I'll add in a reply to this comment.)

records.text: Great Splash Singapore event! “Strategy is no longer about predicting the future; it’s about building optionality for different futures.” This takeaway of SPLASH Singapore strongly resonates with the challenge of decarbonising shipping. With the future fuel mix still uncertain, the answer may not be to bet everything on a single fuel today. It may also be about reducing our dependence on any fuel. This is precisely where wind-assisted propulsion can make a difference: by harnessing a renewable energy source that is available today and independent of the fuel used on board. By reducing a vessel’s energy demand, wind assistance can help: - Limit exposure to fuel prices and availability; - Mitigate long-term technology risks; - Improve the performance of multiple fuel pathways; - Preserve flexibility in an uncertain regulatory environment. Wind-assisted propulsion is therefore more than a decarbonisation solution. It is also a way to build strategic optionality. In an uncertain future, could one of the smartest choices simply be to need less fuel—whatever that fuel may be? #Maritime #Shipping #WindAssistedPropulsion #Decarbonisation #EnergyTransition #SPLASHSingapore

records.title: Vijeta Tantry
records.text: In 1936, Sarla Thakral became the first Indian woman to earn a pilot's licence. Ninety years later, her photograph hangs on our wall, and the company that carries her name is building India's electric air taxi. For the first chapter of Women in Aviation @ Sarla, we sat down with six of the women designing and building it. They spoke about being one of five or six women in an aerospace engineering class. They spoke about growing up in a tier two city where no one knew a career in aviation was possible, and about why so few women stay in core technology roles. And they spoke about what it takes to design an aircraft, which one of them compared to raising a child: every structure, every sub-component, every detail from birth. What stayed with all of them was Sarla herself. As one of them put it, "She walked the path so that we can run on it." Thank you to Vijeta Tantry , Payal Satish , Nishtha Sharma , Pavana Prabhu , Saisurya Anbazhagan Vanniyar and Medha Deshpande for sharing your stories. #WomenInAviation #SarlaAviation #eVTOL #Aerospace

records.text: Иногда на собеседовании можно удивить даже Senior-разработчика. Примерно полгода назад проходил собеседование на позицию Backend Developer внутри Сбера. Разговор зашёл о Kafka и consumer groups. Обсуждали ситуацию, когда одна consumer group читает несколько топиков. А точнее вред такого подхода. Я упомянул интересный нюанс: ошибка или нестабильность consumer'а, возникшая при работе с одним топиком, может привести к rebalance и повлиять на обработку других топиков той же consumer group. С подобным я сталкивался на практике. Вал ошибок, который ни с того ни с сего возник при вычитке топика, который давно никто не трогал, был связан как раз с такой проблемой. Собеседующий сначала не поверил и подумал, что я что-то путаю. Он был уверен, что ребалансировка не может выходить за пределы одного топика. В итоге я оказался прав.🕺😁 Для меня это был хороший пример того, что собеседование не только проверяет твои знания. Иногда ты сам можешь принести на интервью что-то новое для собеседующего.

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors performed exactly to spec. Fused together, the vehicle's obstacle map kept ghosting — objects appearing, shifting eleven centimeters, then reappearing a few feet away. The bug wasn't in either sensor. It was in the extrinsic calibration — the rigid transform describing where each sensor sits relative to the vehicle's reference frame. That transform had been measured once, on a bench, before the vehicle ever left the shop. After a week of field testing — vibration, a few hard stops, one rougher-than-planned landing — one mount had rotated by a fraction of a degree. Invisible to the eye. Invisible on a close-range bench check. But rotational error doesn't behave like translational error. A pure positional shift between two sensors stays roughly constant no matter how far away the target is. A rotational shift scales directly with range — a fifth of a degree of tilt is nothing at arm's length and eleven centimeters of disagreement at thirty meters. That's exactly the kind of drift a bench calibration at close range will never catch, and a mid-range operational test will always find. Individually-passing sensors don't buy you a passing fusion stack. The fix wasn't algorithmic — it was adding an online extrinsic self-check that flags when the sensors' overlapping field of view stops agreeing, before it becomes an obstacle-avoidance decision. Small businesses building perception stacks should treat that self-check as a requirement, not a nice-to-have. It's usually the difference between a DT&E finding you catch yourself and one the government catches for you. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.text: Организация Archer поделилась обновлением: Air traffic control (ATC) still runs on one of the oldest live communication mediums: bandwidth-limited AM radio, spoken in rapid, dense phraseology, where every instruction vanishes the moment it is heard. As a pilot, I witness the operational challenges that come with ATC communications firsthand. Today we're publishing a deep dive into the speech capability of ZEE, Archer's proprietary aviation foundation model. General-purpose models struggle with harsh radio acoustics and restricted jargon, and are unable to understand the nuances of aviation navigational terminology. For example the word "stick" near San Francisco is the SSTIK departure, while "stick" in North Carolina is spelled as STIKK. That nuance is not in the audio, and decoding that signal requires more than just good speech recognition. So we built ZEE differently: — A single speech engine that collapses voice activity detection, speaker diarization, and transcription into one model, emitting one speaker-attributed token stream. — Spatial grounding that injects location context so the model correctly transcribes local waypoints and procedures in any airspace. — A language model that decomposes each dense transmission into discrete, structured, verifiable commands. The result: 84% better accuracy than general-purpose speech models on aviation audio, and a 58% reduction in entity transcription errors from spatial grounding. All of it running in real time, offline, and on-device; so that pilots and controllers alike can benefit from this layer of intelligence. Every radio call becomes a permanent, scrollable, time-indexed record. And it lays the foundation for what comes next: catching readback errors and communication breakdowns in real time, before a misheard clearance becomes an incident. The next era of aviation safety should begin where it matters most: in cockpits and air traffic control towers. Preventing tragic, avoidable accidents starts by making communication clear and effortless in the sky. This is one of the missions behind ZEE, and behind everything my extraordinary team builds: a world where every single flight reaches its destination safely. Full post: https://lnkd.in/dvauVg2E.

records.text: Организация Department of Aerospace Science and Technology - Politecnico di Milano разместила контент: How closely do particles follow rotor-induced flow before reaching a blade? New research by Francesco Caccia and Alberto Guardone investigates the dynamics of inertial particles in rotor-induced flows, considering both a wind turbine and a small-scale propeller. The study shows that the key lies in how the particle response time compares with the characteristic time scale of the induced flow. The authors introduce an induction Stokes number to identify the transition between particles that follow the induced velocity field and those that are essentially unaffected by it. A reduced-order analytical model is then developed to capture this delayed particle response, providing corrected conditions for 2-D sectional simulations and reproducing the transition observed in full 3-D simulations. The results have implications for modelling multiphase rotor flows, including applications involving icing and particle-induced erosion. Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors performed exactly to spec. Fused together, the vehicle's obstacle map kept ghosting — objects appearing, shifting eleven centimeters, then reappearing a few feet away. The bug wasn't in either sensor. It was in the extrinsic calibration — the rigid transform describing where each sensor sits relative to the vehicle's reference frame. That transform had been measured once, on a bench, before the vehicle ever left the shop. After a week of field testing — vibration, a few hard stops, one rougher-than-planned landing — one mount had rotated by a fraction of a degree. Invisible to the eye. Invisible on a close-range bench check. But rotational error doesn't behave like translational error. A pure positional shift between two sensors stays roughly constant no matter how far away the target is. A rotational shift scales directly with range — a fifth of a degree of tilt is nothing at arm's length and eleven centimeters of disagreement at thirty meters. That's exactly the kind of drift a bench calibration at close range will never catch, and a mid-range operational test will always find. Individually-passing sensors don't buy you a passing fusion stack. The fix wasn't algorithmic — it was adding an online extrinsic self-check that flags when the sensors' overlapping field of view stops agreeing, before it becomes an obstacle-avoidance decision. Small businesses building perception stacks should treat that self-check as a requirement, not a nice-to-have. It's usually the difference between a DT&E finding you catch yourself and one the government catches for you. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Today we're publishing a deep dive into the speech capability of ZEE, Archer's proprietary aviation foundation model. General-purpose models struggle with harsh radio acoustics and restricted jargon, and are unable to understand the nuances of aviation navigational terminology.
